item.title: Forty Drones Over One City: Inside the Siege the UN Calls a Warning Sign for Mass Atrocities
item.body:
## A City Under Near-Daily Bombardment

For months, residents of el-Obeid, the capital of Sudan's North Kordofan state, have described a grim daily routine: the distant buzz of drones overhead, followed by the wait to see where the next strike will land. Humanitarian monitors tracking the conflict say the city has absorbed dozens of drone attacks in a matter of weeks — by some counts, roughly forty strikes have hit the area — as fighting between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) grinds through its third year.

El-Obeid sits at a strategic crossroads linking Khartoum to Sudan's western regions, which is part of why it has become a flashpoint. Aid workers say the city has effectively been under siege, with supply routes choked off and civilians caught between advancing front lines.

## Hospitals Knocked Out of Service

Among the most alarming consequences, according to humanitarian organizations operating in the area, is the damage inflicted on el-Obeid's already-strained health system. Strikes attributed to the ongoing fighting have reportedly hit or forced the closure of medical facilities, stripping the city of capacity just as civilian casualties and disease outbreaks are rising. The World Health Organization and Sudanese medical unions have repeatedly warned that attacks on hospitals violate international humanitarian law, regardless of which side is responsible, and that a functioning health system is often the difference between a contained outbreak and a public health catastrophe.

With fuel, medicine and staff in short supply, doctors on the ground say they are being forced to make impossible choices about who receives treatment — a situation aid groups describe as unsustainable if the bombardment continues at its current pace.

## Cholera Spreads as Water Systems Fail

Compounding the crisis, health officials have confirmed a spreading cholera outbreak in and around el-Obeid. Cholera thrives where clean water and sanitation infrastructure has broken down — conditions that sieges and displacement reliably produce. Aid agencies report that damaged water systems, overcrowded displacement sites, and the collapse of routine health services have created ideal conditions for the waterborne disease to take hold.

Sudan has recorded cholera cases in multiple states since the civil war reignited in 2023, but responders say the situation in North Kordofan is especially difficult to manage because access for aid convoys remains severely restricted, limiting the delivery of oral rehydration supplies, chlorine tablets and vaccines.

## The UN's Warning: A Pattern That Precedes Atrocities

United Nations officials monitoring Sudan have pointed to el-Obeid as an example of a broader and deeply concerning pattern: repeated strikes on civilian infrastructure, blocked humanitarian access, and the targeting of essential services in besieged areas. UN representatives have cautioned that this combination of tactics — documented elsewhere in Sudan's war, including in Darfur — has historically preceded some of the gravest violations of international law, and they have urged both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF to allow unimpeded humanitarian access and to protect civilians and medical facilities under international humanitarian law.

Human rights researchers note that sieges which cut off food, water, fuel and medicine can constitute collective punishment of civilian populations, a serious violation regardless of the military objectives claimed by the parties involved. The UN has called for independent investigations into strikes on hospitals and for accountability mechanisms to be strengthened as the conflict continues.

## A Wider Humanitarian Emergency

Sudan's civil war has already produced one of the world's largest displacement crises, with the UN estimating that millions of people have fled their homes since fighting began in April 2023. El-Obeid's situation reflects a broader trend across contested areas of the country, where famine conditions, disease outbreaks and attacks on civilian infrastructure have converged.

International aid organizations have appealed for expanded humanitarian corridors and increased funding, warning that without a sustained ceasefire and guaranteed access for relief workers, cities like el-Obeid risk becoming case studies in how modern sieges can escalate into humanitarian catastrophes. For now, residents say they are left to weather both the drones overhead and the disease spreading in the shadows below — waiting for a diplomatic breakthrough that, so far, has remained out of reach.
